prompt: A company uses AWS Organizations with prod, security and sandbox OUs. Developers in workload accounts must launch EC2 instances from approved AMIs, but the security team's incident-response role must still be able to launch its own forensic AMIs in every account. What is the best guardrail?

options.text: An SCP on the workload OUs that denies ec2:RunInstances unless ec2:ImageID is an approved AMI, exempting that role by aws:PrincipalArn.
A permissions boundary on each developer role that allows ec2:RunInstances for approved AMI IDs, attached by the platform team's pipeline.
options.explanation: A boundary binds the roles it is attached to; an account admin can create a new role without it, so it is not an account-wide guardrail.

options.text: The AWS Config managed rule approved-amis-by-id in a conformance pack, with SSM Automation remediation that terminates noncompliant instances.
options.explanation: Config is detective: the instance launches and runs until remediation fires, so it does not prevent the launch.

options.text: A tag policy requiring an ApprovedImage tag on EC2 instances, with enforcement enabled for the ec2:instance resource type in the workload OUs.
options.explanation: A tag policy checks the tag's value when the tag is set; it never inspects which AMI the instance was launched from.

explanation: An SCP is a preventive control that applies to every principal in the member accounts, account admins included, so a Deny on ec2:RunInstances conditioned on ec2:ImageID enforces the approved list, and an aws:PrincipalArn condition exempts the incident-response role. A Config rule only reacts after launch, a permissions boundary binds only the roles it is attached to, and a tag policy validates tags, not images. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps_examples.html

prompt: A regulated company needs CloudTrail logs from every account in its organization collected centrally, where administrators of the member accounts cannot stop the logging or alter or delete the delivered logs. Which design best meets this?

options.text: An organization trail delivering to an S3 bucket in a dedicated log archive account, with a bucket policy that denies object deletion.
A trail in each member account, deployed by a StackSet, delivering to the log archive bucket with read access for the security team.
options.explanation: Member-account admins own their account trails and can stop or delete them, so collection is not protected from them.

options.text: Account trails in each member account sending events to a central CloudWatch Logs destination through cross-account subscriptions.
options.explanation: The trails still live in the member accounts, so their admins can stop them; the central copy only holds what was sent.

options.text: An organization trail with log file integrity validation, delivering to a bucket owned by the member account that runs the regulated workload.
options.explanation: Integrity validation detects tampering after the fact; a bucket in that member account is still under its admins' control.

explanation: An organization trail is created from the management account (or a delegated admin) and member accounts can see it but cannot stop or modify it. Delivering to a bucket in a separate log archive account keeps the logs out of member admins' reach, and the bucket policy blocks deletion. Per-account trails can be stopped by the account's own admins, and integrity validation only detects changes. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/creating-trail-organization.html

prompt: An enterprise wants account vending with a mandatory VPC baseline, IAM Identity Center access, centralized logging and detective controls in every new account, while writing as little custom code as possible. What should it use?

options.text: AWS Control Tower with Account Factory, adding the VPC baseline through Account Factory Customization blueprints.
CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions and automatic deployment to new accounts in each OU.
options.explanation: StackSets deploy templates, but the team must still write and maintain the logging, Identity Center and control baselines itself.

options.text: An Organizations CreateAccount pipeline in Step Functions that applies Terraform baselines and enrolls the account in Identity Center.
options.explanation: Every part of this is custom code the team must build and maintain, which is what the requirement asks to avoid.

options.text: AWS Service Catalog portfolios shared to each OU, with a product that provisions the VPC, a log bucket and Config rules.
options.explanation: Service Catalog provisions products into existing accounts; it does not create accounts or set up the landing zone around them.

explanation: Control Tower sets up the landing zone (log archive and audit accounts, centralized CloudTrail and Config, IAM Identity Center) and its Account Factory vends accounts with preventive and detective controls applied; Account Factory Customization adds a VPC baseline from a blueprint. StackSets and Service Catalog are building blocks the team would assemble itself, and a Step Functions pipeline is all custom code. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/controltower/latest/userguide/af-customization-page.html

prompt: A company has 120 VPCs across 30 accounts and two on-premises data centers. VPCs need east-west and on-premises connectivity, and all of that traffic must pass through firewall appliances in one central inspection VPC. Which architecture best meets this with the least operational effort?

options.text: One Transit Gateway with spoke and inspection route tables, spokes routing to the inspection VPC attachment in appliance mode.
One Transit Gateway with a single shared route table propagating each attachment, and a firewall appliance in each spoke VPC.
options.explanation: This spreads the firewalls into every spoke instead of inspecting centrally, and one route table cannot force traffic through inspection.

options.text: VPC peering from each spoke to a central inspection VPC, with the Direct Connect gateway associated with that inspection VPC.
options.explanation: Peering is not transitive, so spoke-to-spoke traffic cannot route through the hub VPC's appliances.

options.text: A Transit Gateway in each account, each peered to a hub Transit Gateway in the network account that attaches the inspection VPC.
options.explanation: Thirty TGWs with static routes on each peering add cost and operational load with no benefit over one shared TGW.

explanation: A single Transit Gateway, shared through AWS RAM, scales to hundreds of VPC attachments. Separate route tables send spoke and on-premises traffic to the inspection VPC attachment, and appliance mode keeps both directions of a flow on the same appliance so stateful inspection works. Peering is not transitive, distributed firewalls are not central inspection, and per-account TGWs multiply the routing to maintain. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/how-transit-gateways-work.html

prompt: A vendor runs a SaaS API in its own VPC and wants customers in other AWS accounts to call it over private IP addresses. Many customer VPCs use CIDR ranges that overlap the vendor's, and the vendor wants to expose the API port without giving customers a route into its network. What should the vendor provide?

options.text: A VPC endpoint service backed by a Network Load Balancer, reached through interface endpoints in each consumer VPC.
A Transit Gateway shared through AWS RAM, with each customer VPC attached and route tables limited to the API subnet.
options.explanation: Routing through a TGW needs non-overlapping CIDRs and still gives customers a network path into the vendor VPC.

options.text: A VPC peering connection with each customer VPC, with security groups that allow the API port from the peer's CIDR.
options.explanation: Peering cannot be created between VPCs with overlapping CIDR blocks, and it exposes a network route.

options.text: An AWS Site-to-Site VPN from each customer VPC to the vendor's Transit Gateway, advertising only the API subnet.
options.explanation: A VPN is routed connectivity, so overlapping CIDRs break it and customers get a path into the vendor network.

explanation: AWS PrivateLink exposes one service, not a network: the provider publishes an endpoint service behind an NLB, and each consumer creates an interface endpoint with IPs from its own subnets. Traffic is initiated one way and never routed between the VPCs, so overlapping CIDRs do not matter. Peering, TGW and VPN all create routed connectivity that requires unique CIDRs. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/privatelink-share-your-services.html

prompt: Two Regions each have a Transit Gateway with many attached VPCs. Applications need private inter-Region connectivity over the AWS network, and each Region's network must stay an independent failure domain. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Peer the two transit gateways and add static routes for the remote Region's CIDRs to each Transit Gateway route table.
Peer the two transit gateways and enable route propagation on the peering attachment so remote CIDRs are learned.
options.explanation: Transit Gateway peering attachments do not support dynamic route propagation; routes over a peering must be static.

options.text: Attach the VPCs in the second Region directly to the first Region's transit gateway, so one TGW routes both Regions.
options.explanation: A Transit Gateway attaches VPCs in its own Region only, and one shared TGW would remove the independent failure domains.

options.text: Connect the two transit gateways with Site-to-Site VPN attachments over the internet, using BGP to exchange routes.
options.explanation: This works but runs over the internet and adds VPN throughput limits; TGW peering uses the encrypted AWS backbone.

explanation: Inter-Region Transit Gateway peering keeps each Region's TGW independent and carries traffic on the AWS global network, encrypted. Peering attachments do not propagate routes, so each TGW route table needs static routes for the remote CIDRs pointing at the peering attachment. A TGW cannot attach VPCs in another Region, and VPN between TGWs is the internet-based fallback, not the recommended design. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/tgw-peering.html

prompt: A 200 TB Oracle database must move to Amazon RDS for Oracle with less than 1 hour of downtime at cutover. The source stays fully active and keeps taking writes until the cutover starts. Which strategy fits best?

options.text: AWS DMS full load followed by ongoing change data capture, cutting over once replication lag is close to zero.
Restore an RMAN backup from Amazon S3 into the RDS for Oracle instance at the start of the outage window.
options.explanation: RDS for Oracle does not support restoring RMAN backups, and a 200 TB restore would not fit in an hour anyway.

options.text: Oracle Data Pump export to S3, imported into RDS through the S3 integration during the outage window.
options.explanation: Data Pump can seed the target, but a 200 TB export and import is far longer than a 1-hour window.

options.text: AWS DMS full load only, scheduled to start when writes are stopped at the beginning of the outage window.
options.explanation: Without CDC the whole 200 TB has to copy inside the outage window, which cannot finish in an hour.

explanation: With a full load plus CDC task, DMS copies the existing data while the source stays live, then its change data capture applies ongoing changes from the redo logs until replication lag is close to zero; the outage is only the time to stop writes, let the last changes apply and switch connections. Backup or export approaches move all 200 TB inside the window, and RDS for Oracle cannot restore RMAN backups. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/dms/latest/userguide/CHAP_Task.CDC.html

prompt: A monolith on EC2 behind an Application Load Balancer is being modernized gradually. The team wants requests for /checkout to go to a new container service while every other path stays on the monolith, under the same domain name. Which approach fits best?

options.text: An ALB listener rule with a path condition for /checkout* forwarding to the container service's target group.
ALB weighted target groups on the default rule, shifting a percentage of requests to the container service.
options.explanation: Weighted target groups split all requests by percentage; they cannot send one path to the new service.

options.text: A Route 53 record for a new checkout subdomain pointing at the container service, keeping the main domain on the monolith.
options.explanation: DNS routes by name, not by URL path, so this changes the URLs clients use instead of routing /checkout.

options.text: A Network Load Balancer listener per service, with target groups splitting /checkout from the other paths.
options.explanation: An NLB works at layer 4 and cannot see HTTP paths, so it has no way to route on /checkout.

explanation: ALB listener rules evaluate layer-7 conditions such as path patterns, so a rule for /checkout* can forward to the new service while the default rule keeps sending everything else to the monolith: the strangler-fig pattern. Weighted target groups split traffic by percentage, Route 53 cannot route on paths, and an NLB has no view of HTTP. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/rule-condition-types.html

prompt: A data center holds 300 TB of archived files on an NFS server. A 10 Gbps Direct Connect connection is in place. The files must land in Amazon S3 within a month, keeping their POSIX metadata, with every file's integrity verified after transfer. What should be the primary transfer mechanism?

options.text: AWS DataSync agents on premises sending over Direct Connect to a DataSync VPC endpoint, with data verification on.
An Amazon S3 File Gateway mounted on premises, with the files copied to its NFS share and uploaded to S3 in the background.
options.explanation: File Gateway is built for ongoing hybrid access through a local cache; for a one-time bulk move AWS points to DataSync.

options.text: The AWS CLI running parallel aws s3 sync jobs from several on-premises hosts over a Direct Connect public VIF.
options.explanation: aws s3 sync does not carry POSIX ownership and permissions and has no end-to-end verification of the copied files.

options.text: An AWS Transfer Family SFTP server with a VPC endpoint, receiving the files from on-premises scripts over Direct Connect.
options.explanation: Transfer Family is for partner file exchange over SFTP; it does not preserve POSIX metadata or verify a bulk copy.

explanation: DataSync is the managed service for moving file data into S3: agents read the NFS share in parallel, traffic can use Direct Connect to a VPC endpoint, POSIX metadata is stored with the objects, and the task verifies data after transfer. 300 TB at a sustained few Gbps fits in a month. S3 File Gateway is for ongoing cached access, and the CLI and SFTP options lose metadata and verification. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datasync/latest/userguide/what-is-datasync.html

prompt: An application must recover from a Region failure with an RTO of 5 minutes and an RPO of seconds. It uses Aurora PostgreSQL and a stateless web tier. Which design best meets this?

options.text: Aurora Global Database with a secondary Region, a scaled-down web tier running there, and Route 53 failover records.
AWS Backup copying Aurora snapshots to the second Region every hour, with the web tier pre-deployed and scaled to zero.
options.explanation: Hourly snapshot copies give an RPO of up to an hour, and restoring a cluster from a snapshot takes far longer than 5 minutes.

options.text: AWS DMS ongoing replication to a standby Aurora cluster in the second Region, with Route 53 failover records.
options.explanation: DMS replication adds lag and a task to operate; Aurora Global Database replicates at the storage layer with typical lag under a second.

options.text: Aurora Global Database with a headless secondary cluster, and the web tier deployed by CloudFormation after failover.
options.explanation: Adding a DB instance to a headless cluster and deploying the web stack both take tens of minutes, beyond a 5-minute RTO.

explanation: Aurora Global Database replicates storage to a secondary Region with typical lag under a second, and a secondary cluster that already has a reader instance can be promoted in minutes. Keeping a scaled-down web tier running there (warm standby) and failing DNS over with Route 53 health checks fits a 5-minute RTO. Snapshots miss the RPO, DMS adds lag, and a headless pilot light misses the RTO. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-global-database-disaster-recovery.html

prompt: A workload needs cross-Region disaster recovery with an RTO of 4 hours and an RPO of 24 hours, at the lowest ongoing cost. Which recovery strategy fits best?

options.text: Backup and restore: daily backups copied to the DR Region, with infrastructure as code to rebuild the stack there.
Pilot light: data replicated continuously to the DR Region, core services in place, app servers switched off until needed.
options.explanation: Pilot light buys an RTO of tens of minutes and an RPO of minutes, at an ongoing cost the 4-hour and 24-hour targets do not need.

options.text: Warm standby: a scaled-down but fully working copy of the stack running in the DR Region, scaled out on failover.
options.explanation: Warm standby keeps a running copy of the stack, which costs far more than these relaxed objectives require.

options.text: Multi-site active/active: both Regions serve traffic, with data replicated and Route 53 sending users to either Region.
options.explanation: Active/active gives near-zero RTO and RPO at the highest cost; nothing in the requirements calls for it.

explanation: The AWS DR strategies trade cost against recovery objectives: backup and restore is the cheapest and fits RPO/RTO measured in hours, pilot light and warm standby keep replicated data and some or all of the stack running for tens-of-minutes or minutes RTO, and multi-site active/active targets near zero. A 24-hour RPO is met by daily cross-Region backup copies, and IaC rebuilds the stack within 4 hours. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html

prompt: A multi-Region active-active API keeps account balances in Amazon DynamoDB in three Regions. A client that writes in one Region and then reads in another must see its own write, and every conditional update must be checked against the latest balance, whichever Region receives it. Which design meets this?

options.text: DynamoDB global tables in multi-Region strong consistency mode, with strongly consistent reads and conditional writes.
DynamoDB global tables in the default multi-Region eventual consistency mode, with conditional writes on a version attribute.
options.explanation: With eventual consistency a condition is checked against the local replica only, and concurrent writes resolve last-writer-wins.

options.text: A DynamoDB table in one Region, with DAX clusters in the other two Regions serving reads and forwarding writes.
options.explanation: A DAX cluster must run in the same Region as its table, so it cannot front a table in another Region.

options.text: Separate DynamoDB tables in each Region, with DynamoDB Streams and Lambda replicating each change to the others.
options.explanation: Custom stream replication is asynchronous, so a read in another Region can miss a recent write.

explanation: Global tables configured for multi-Region strong consistency (MRSC) replicate each write synchronously to at least one other Region before acknowledging it, so a strongly consistent read in any Region returns the latest item and conditions are evaluated against it. The default eventual consistency mode replicates asynchronously, typically within a second, and resolves conflicts last-writer-wins, which fails both requirements. MRSC is deployed across exactly three Regions. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/V2globaltables_HowItWorks.html

prompt: A SaaS platform stores every tenant's objects in one shared S3 bucket under a per-tenant prefix. The security team needs tenant isolation that still holds if the application code has a bug that requests the wrong tenant's key. What is the best additional control?

options.text: Session tags carrying the tenant ID, and a policy allowing S3 object actions on the ${aws:PrincipalTag/tenant}/* prefix.
An S3 access point per tenant, with the application choosing the access point from the tenant ID in each request.
options.explanation: The application still chooses the access point, so the same bug that picks the wrong key can pick the wrong access point.

options.text: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key per tenant, chosen by the application when it writes each object.
options.explanation: The application role needs access to every tenant's key, so a buggy request is still authorized to decrypt the wrong tenant's data.

options.text: Amazon Macie scanning the bucket daily and alerting when an object's tenant tag does not match its prefix.
options.explanation: Macie finds sensitive data after the fact; it does not stop a request from reading another tenant's objects.

explanation: With attribute-based access control, the application assumes a role with a session tag for the authenticated tenant, and the policy resource uses ${aws:PrincipalTag/tenant}, so IAM itself refuses any key outside that tenant's prefix whatever the code asks for. Access points and per-tenant keys still depend on the application choosing correctly, and Macie is detective. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_session-tags.html

prompt: A workload in private subnets with no route to the internet retrieves secrets from AWS Secrets Manager and also calls AWS KMS directly to encrypt data. Security forbids NAT gateways for this traffic. What should be added?

options.text: Interface VPC endpoints for Secrets Manager and KMS in the workload subnets, with private DNS enabled on both.
Gateway VPC endpoints for Secrets Manager and KMS, added to the route tables of the workload subnets.
options.explanation: Gateway endpoints exist for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB alone; Secrets Manager and KMS are reached through interface endpoints.

options.text: An interface endpoint for Secrets Manager alone, relying on Secrets Manager to call KMS for the workload.
options.explanation: Secrets Manager calls KMS for its own decryption, but the workload's direct KMS calls still need a KMS endpoint.

options.text: A KMS custom key store in AWS CloudHSM inside the VPC, so key operations stay on private addresses.
options.explanation: Requests still go to the KMS API endpoint; the custom key store changes where keys live, not how the workload reaches KMS.

explanation: Secrets Manager and KMS are reached privately through interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink), and private DNS makes the default service hostnames resolve to the endpoint IPs so SDKs need no changes. Because the workload calls KMS itself, it needs a KMS endpoint as well as the Secrets Manager one. Gateway endpoints exist for S3 and DynamoDB, and a CloudHSM key store is still used through the KMS API. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/aws-services-privatelink-support.html

prompt: Compliance logs from all accounts are archived in a bucket in a log archive account. Administrators of that account manage the bucket, but auditors require that they cannot read the logs unless the security team, which runs a separate security account, approves. Which design best meets this?

options.text: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key held in the security account, whose key policy allows decrypt for one approved role.
SSE-KMS with a customer managed key in the log archive account, its key policy limiting decrypt to a security role.
options.explanation: The key lives in the account its admins control, so they can change the key policy and grant themselves decrypt.

options.text: SSE-S3 encryption, with a bucket policy that denies s3:GetObject to every principal except the security team's role.
options.explanation: The log archive admins manage the bucket policy, so they can edit it; SSE-S3 adds no separate control over decryption.

options.text: SSE-KMS with the AWS managed key aws/s3, plus an SCP that denies kms:Decrypt in the log archive account to non-security roles.
options.explanation: An AWS managed key cannot be used from another account, so writers elsewhere and the security account cannot use it.

explanation: Putting the customer managed key in the security account separates the two duties: log archive admins can manage the bucket, but reading an object needs kms:Decrypt on a key whose policy only the security account can change. A key in the log archive account, or a bucket-policy-only control, leaves the same admins able to grant themselves access, and AWS managed keys cannot be shared across accounts. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/key-policy-modifying-external-accounts.html

prompt: Reports run heavy aggregations over five years of order history in an Aurora MySQL cluster and join it with clickstream data already in Amazon Redshift. The reports slow production, may be up to 30 minutes stale, and the team wants no ETL pipeline to maintain. Which approach fits best?

options.text: An Aurora zero-ETL integration with Amazon Redshift, with the reports moved to run in the Redshift warehouse.
An Aurora Replica behind a custom reader endpoint for the reports, joined to clickstream through Redshift federated queries.
options.explanation: The heavy aggregations still run on a row-oriented MySQL replica, and federated queries pull the rows across for every report.

options.text: AWS Glue jobs exporting the order tables to S3 every 15 minutes, queried with the clickstream through Redshift Spectrum.
options.explanation: This works, but it is exactly the ETL pipeline the team wants to avoid building and maintaining.

options.text: Aurora parallel query enabled on the production cluster, with the clickstream data loaded into Aurora for the joins.
options.explanation: Parallel query still runs on the production cluster, and loading clickstream into Aurora is itself an ETL job.

explanation: A zero-ETL integration replicates Aurora MySQL data into Redshift within seconds without a pipeline to build, so the reports run as columnar warehouse queries next to the clickstream data and stop competing with OLTP traffic. A reader endpoint offloads the writer but leaves large scans on MySQL, and Glue exports or parallel query either add ETL or keep the load on production. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/zero-etl.html

prompt: A clickstream pipeline ingests millions of events per minute. Four teams each need to read the full stream independently at their own pace, and any team must be able to reprocess the last 7 days after fixing a bug. Which design fits best?

options.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with retention raised to 7 days and an enhanced fan-out consumer for each team.
An Amazon SNS topic fanning out to an SQS queue per team, with message retention set to 14 days on each queue.
options.explanation: Retention only keeps unconsumed messages; once a team processes and deletes a message it cannot be read again.

options.text: Kinesis Data Streams with the default 24-hour retention, read by one shared consumer that fans out to each team.
options.explanation: The default retention is 24 hours, so a 7-day reprocess is impossible, and one shared consumer couples the teams.

options.text: An SQS FIFO queue per team, with the producer writing each event to all four queues in the same message group.
options.explanation: FIFO throughput is far below millions of events per minute in one message group, and consumed messages cannot be replayed.

explanation: Kinesis Data Streams keeps records for a configurable retention period (24 hours by default, up to 365 days), so each consumer tracks its own position and can rewind to replay. Enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer its own read throughput. SQS-based fan-out deletes messages once consumed, so there is nothing to replay. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/kinesis-extended-retention.html

prompt: A data lake in S3 needs central governance over its tables, column-level permissions so analysts cannot see PII columns, and access for analysts in other AWS accounts. What should be used?

options.text: AWS Lake Formation grants on Data Catalog tables, with data filters for columns and LF-Tags shared to analyst accounts.
S3 Access Grants mapping each analyst group to the tables' S3 prefixes, with grants issued to roles in the analyst accounts.
options.explanation: Access Grants control access to S3 prefixes and objects; they cannot hide individual columns inside a table's files.

options.text: IAM policies on the analyst roles plus S3 bucket policies granting cross-account read on the table prefixes.
options.explanation: IAM and bucket policies grant whole objects, so any analyst who can read a file can read every column in it.

options.text: Glue Data Catalog resource policies granting cross-account access to the tables, with S3 bucket policies for the data.
options.explanation: Catalog resource policies work at database and table level and the bucket policy grants whole files, so columns stay exposed.

explanation: Lake Formation adds fine-grained permissions on top of the Glue Data Catalog: data filters restrict columns and rows, LF-Tags scale grants, and cross-account sharing goes through AWS RAM, with Athena, Redshift Spectrum and EMR enforcing it. The other options all grant at object or table level, so whoever can read a file sees every column in it. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lake-formation/latest/dg/data-filtering.html

prompt: A steady EC2 fleet runs 24/7 across several instance families in one Region. Teams change instance sizes and families often, and over the next year they plan to move part of the fleet to AWS Fargate. Which commitment fits best for the steady baseline?

options.text: Compute Savings Plans sized to the baseline, leaving any usage above the commitment on On-Demand.
EC2 Instance Savings Plans for each current instance family, sized to that family's share of the baseline.
options.explanation: EC2 Instance Savings Plans are tied to one family in one Region, so they stop applying when teams switch families or move to Fargate.

options.text: Convertible Reserved Instances for the baseline, exchanged for new instance families as teams resize.
options.explanation: Convertible RIs can be exchanged across families but never cover Fargate, and each change needs a manual exchange.

options.text: Regional Standard Reserved Instances for the current families, sold on the RI Marketplace if needs change.
options.explanation: Standard RIs are fixed to a family, cannot cover Fargate, and resale on the Marketplace is not guaranteed.

explanation: Compute Savings Plans apply automatically to EC2 usage of any family, size, OS or Region, and also to Fargate and Lambda, so the discount follows the fleet as it changes. EC2 Instance Savings Plans give a deeper discount but are locked to one family in one Region, and Reserved Instances of either type do not cover Fargate. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/savingsplans/latest/userguide/plan-types.html

prompt: Workers process jobs from an SQS queue; jobs can be interrupted and retried. Demand spikes unpredictably. The company wants the lowest compute cost while keeping jobs completing during Spot capacity shortages. Which design is best?

options.text: Spot across many instance types and AZs with price-capacity-optimized allocation, a small On-Demand base, idempotent workers.
Spot with the lowest-price allocation strategy across two instance types in three AZs, with workers checkpointing to S3.
options.explanation: Lowest-price with two types packs capacity into the cheapest pools, which are the ones most likely to be interrupted.

options.text: A Compute Savings Plan sized to peak demand, with workers on On-Demand instances in an Auto Scaling group.
options.explanation: A commitment sized to an unpredictable peak pays for idle capacity most of the time; it is not the lowest cost.

options.text: Spot in a single AZ with capacity-optimized allocation across many types, scaled on the queue depth.
options.explanation: One AZ limits the number of Spot pools to draw from, so a shortage in that zone can stall every worker.

explanation: Interruptible queue workers suit Spot. Diversifying across many instance types and AZs, with the price-capacity-optimized strategy, draws from the deepest pools at a low price; a small On-Demand base keeps jobs moving during shortages, and idempotent workers make retries safe. Lowest-price with few types, a single AZ, or a peak-sized commitment each fail on interruption risk or cost. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/allocation-strategies.html

prompt: Objects in an S3 data lake are read heavily for 30 days, then a few times a week for the next 90 days with millisecond access, then almost never, but must be kept for 7 years; retrieval within 12 hours is acceptable by then. The data cannot be regenerated, and access is predictable. Which plan costs least?

options.text: Lifecycle rules: S3 Standard, to Standard-IA at day 30, to Glacier Deep Archive at day 120, expiring after 7 years.
Lifecycle rules: S3 Standard, to One Zone-IA at day 30, to Glacier Deep Archive at day 120, expiring after 7 years.
options.explanation: One Zone-IA keeps one copy in a single AZ, which is not acceptable for data that cannot be regenerated.

options.text: S3 Intelligent-Tiering from upload, with the Deep Archive Access tier activated after 180 days without access.
options.explanation: With a known pattern, lifecycle rules reach the cheap classes sooner and avoid Intelligent-Tiering's per-object monitoring fee.

options.text: Lifecycle rules: S3 Standard, to Glacier Flexible Retrieval at day 30, to Glacier Deep Archive at day 120, expiring after 7 years.
options.explanation: Flexible Retrieval restores take minutes to hours, which fails the millisecond access needed during the 90-day period.

explanation: When access is predictable, lifecycle transitions match the storage class to each phase: Standard while hot, Standard-IA (multi-AZ, millisecond access) once objects are 30 days old, Glacier Deep Archive for long retention with retrieval within 12 hours, then expiration at 7 years. One Zone-IA risks data that cannot be recreated, Flexible Retrieval is too slow for the warm phase, and Intelligent-Tiering suits unknown patterns. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html

prompt: Instances in VPCs must resolve names in the on-premises DNS domain, and on-premises servers must resolve names in Route 53 private hosted zones associated with those VPCs. Direct Connect is in place. What is the right hybrid DNS design?

options.text: Inbound Resolver endpoints for queries from on premises, and outbound endpoints with forwarding rules for the on-premises domain.
Outbound endpoints with forwarding rules for the on-premises domain, and on-premises DNS forwarding to each VPC's .2 resolver.
options.explanation: The VPC's .2 resolver only answers queries from inside the VPC, so on-premises servers need an inbound endpoint to reach it.

options.text: Outbound endpoints with forwarding rules, and the private hosted zones associated with the Direct Connect gateway.
options.explanation: Private hosted zones can be associated with VPCs only, not with a Direct Connect gateway or an on-premises network.

options.text: A Route 53 Profile shared to the VPCs with the private hosted zones, and system rules for the on-premises domain.
options.explanation: A Profile shares DNS settings among VPCs, and system rules resolve locally; neither forwards queries to or from on premises.

explanation: Route 53 Resolver handles both directions: an inbound endpoint gives on-premises DNS servers IP addresses in the VPC to forward private-zone queries to, and an outbound endpoint plus a forwarding rule sends queries for the on-premises domain to the on-premises servers. The .2 resolver is not reachable from outside the VPC, and private hosted zones associate only with VPCs. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver.html

prompt: A central security team needs Amazon GuardDuty findings from all accounts in all enabled Regions in one place, with GuardDuty switched on automatically in new accounts. What should they configure?

options.text: A GuardDuty delegated administrator set in each Region, with auto-enable for all organization members turned on in each Region.
A GuardDuty delegated administrator in the home Region with auto-enable, plus Security Hub cross-Region finding aggregation.
options.explanation: GuardDuty is a Regional service: setting it up in one Region leaves the other Regions without detectors to aggregate.

options.text: GuardDuty enabled in the management account in each Region, with member accounts added by invitation from it.
options.explanation: Invitations must be sent and accepted account by account, and AWS advises against running security services from the management account.

options.text: GuardDuty enabled per account by a StackSet with automatic deployment, each account exporting findings to its own S3 bucket.
options.explanation: Findings end up spread across one bucket per account, so the team has no central place to see them.

explanation: GuardDuty is Regional, so the delegated administrator is designated, and organization auto-enable is turned on, in each Region; the admin account then sees findings for all members in that Region, and new accounts are enrolled automatically. Configuring one Region leaves gaps elsewhere, invitations do not scale, and per-account exports are not central. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/guardduty_organizations.html

prompt: A legacy Linux app runs on EC2 instances in two AZs that share an NFSv4 file system for uploaded documents. The first migration phase must leave the app unchanged and replace the self-managed NFS server with a managed service that survives an AZ failure and needs no capacity planning. Which storage target fits best?

options.text: Amazon EFS in Regional mode, mounted over NFS by the instances through a mount target in each AZ.
Amazon FSx for OpenZFS in a Single-AZ deployment, mounted over NFS by the instances in both AZs.
options.explanation: Single-AZ FSx does not survive the loss of its AZ, and FSx needs storage capacity provisioned up front.

options.text: An Amazon EBS io2 volume with Multi-Attach enabled, attached to the instances in both AZs.
options.explanation: Multi-Attach works only within one AZ and needs a cluster-aware file system, not NFS.

options.text: Mountpoint for Amazon S3 on each instance, with the bucket's documents prefix mounted as the shared directory.
options.explanation: Mountpoint does not support editing existing files or file locking, so it does not behave like an NFS share.

explanation: EFS is a managed NFSv4 file system that stores data across multiple AZs in Regional mode and grows and shrinks with the data, so the app mounts it the same way it mounted the old NFS server. Single-AZ FSx does not survive an AZ loss, EBS Multi-Attach is confined to one AZ, and Mountpoint for S3 does not offer full file-system semantics. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/whatisefs.html

prompt: A company runs its workload in one Region using RDS Multi-AZ, EC2 Auto Scaling across three AZs, and S3. The board now requires recovery from a Region-wide outage within 8 hours. What must the architect add?

options.text: Cross-Region copies of the data, infrastructure as code that can build the stack in a second Region, and a tested runbook.
S3 Cross-Region Replication and an RDS cross-Region read replica, relying on the Multi-AZ compute for the rest.
options.explanation: Data would survive, but the compute and networking still exist in the failed Region alone, with nothing ready to run elsewhere.

options.text: A fourth AZ for the Auto Scaling group and an RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster with two readable standbys in the Region.
options.explanation: More AZs and standbys raise availability inside the Region, but all of them fail together in a Region-wide outage.

options.text: AWS Backup plans for RDS, EC2 and S3 with daily backups kept in a locked vault in the same Region.
options.explanation: Backups stored in the same Region are unavailable in a Region-wide outage, and there is no plan to rebuild elsewhere.

explanation: Multi-AZ protects against the loss of an AZ, not a Region. Region-level DR needs the data in a second Region (backup copies or replication), a way to stand up the infrastructure there (IaC), and a failover procedure that has been tested. Replicating data alone, adding AZs, or keeping backups in the same Region each leave one of those missing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html

prompt: A mobile game backend reads and writes player profiles by player ID at tens of thousands of requests per second, with 10x spikes when events start. It needs single-digit millisecond latency, data durable across AZs, no capacity planning and no servers to patch. Which datastore fits best?

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB in on-demand capacity mode, with player ID as the partition key.
Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey as the system of record, with daily snapshots for durability.
options.explanation: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache; writes made since the last snapshot can be lost, so it is not a durable system of record.

options.text: Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 PostgreSQL with player ID as the primary key and Aurora Replicas for reads.
options.explanation: All writes go to one writer instance, and its capacity range and connection limits must be planned for the 10x spikes.

options.text: Amazon S3 with one JSON object per player, using conditional writes to update profiles safely.
options.explanation: S3 request latency is tens of milliseconds, not single-digit, and per-prefix request rates need planning.

explanation: DynamoDB serves key-value reads and writes at single-digit millisecond latency at any scale, replicates across three AZs, and in on-demand mode absorbs sudden spikes with no capacity to plan or servers to manage; a high-cardinality player ID spreads load across partitions. A cache is not durable, Aurora has a single writer to size, and S3 is too slow for this access pattern. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/on-demand-capacity-mode.html

prompt: A NAT gateway bill is unexpectedly high. Most traffic from the private subnets goes to Amazon S3 and DynamoDB in the same Region. What change cuts these charges the most without adding new hourly costs?

options.text: Gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB, added to the route tables of the private subnets.
Interface VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB in each AZ, with private DNS enabled for both services.
options.explanation: Interface endpoints take the traffic off NAT but add an hourly charge per AZ and a per-GB charge; gateway endpoints are free.

options.text: NAT instances on Graviton in each AZ in place of the NAT gateways, keeping the same routes.
options.explanation: The traffic still flows through NAT, now on instances the team must patch and scale; it does not use a private path.

options.text: One NAT gateway in a single AZ shared by the private subnets of the other AZs to cut hourly charges.
options.explanation: Processing charges stay the same, cross-AZ transfer is added, and an AZ failure takes out egress for every subnet.

explanation: Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are route-table targets with no hourly or data processing charge, so traffic to those services leaves the NAT path entirely. Interface endpoints also bypass NAT but are billed per hour and per GB, NAT instances still carry the traffic, and consolidating NAT gateways keeps processing charges while adding cross-AZ transfer and a single point of failure. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/gateway-endpoints.html

prompt: Finance needs monthly cost per application across hundreds of accounts, where several applications share some accounts, and wants chargeback reports without manual spreadsheets. What is the best foundation?

options.text: A tag policy defining the application tag, activated as a cost allocation tag, with Cost Categories built on it for chargeback.
Cost Explorer grouped by linked account, with each account mapped to an application in a monthly export.
options.explanation: Mapping accounts to applications breaks down where several applications share an account.

options.text: AWS Budgets for each account with alerts to application owners, and Budgets reports exported to finance each month.
options.explanation: Budgets track spend against a threshold per account; they do not split a shared account's costs by application.

options.text: Tags applied by IaC, then read with the Resource Groups Tagging API and joined to the cost data by a script.
options.explanation: Tags that are not activated as cost allocation tags never appear in billing data, so this needs a custom join script.

explanation: Cost allocation starts with a consistent tag: a tag policy standardizes the key and values across the organization, activating it as a cost allocation tag makes it appear in Cost Explorer and the cost and usage reports, and Cost Categories group costs into chargeback units with rules, including for shared accounts. Account-level grouping and Budgets cannot split shared accounts, and a tagging-API script rebuilds what billing already offers. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awsaccountbilling/latest/aboutv2/cost-alloc-tags.html

prompt: A public web app with ALB origins in three Regions must block common layer-7 attacks and requests from known malicious IP addresses before that traffic reaches any ALB. Which design fits best?

options.text: A WAF web ACL on a CloudFront distribution in front of the ALBs, using AWS managed rule groups and the IP reputation list.
A regional WAF web ACL on each ALB with the same managed rule groups, kept in sync by AWS Firewall Manager.
options.explanation: The rules run at the ALB itself, so the traffic has already reached it, which the requirement rules out.

options.text: AWS Shield Advanced on the ALBs, with automatic application layer DDoS mitigation turned on.
options.explanation: Shield Advanced protects against DDoS and builds its mitigations with WAF rules; it does not filter SQL injection or bad IPs by itself.

options.text: AWS Network Firewall in an ingress VPC in each Region, with a managed threat signature rule group for known bad hosts.
options.explanation: Network Firewall inspects within each Region's VPC, not at the edge, and is not a web application firewall for HTTP attacks.

explanation: Associating a WAF web ACL with CloudFront evaluates requests at edge locations, before they reach any regional origin. AWS managed rule groups cover common layer-7 attacks, and the Amazon IP reputation list blocks addresses Amazon threat intelligence has identified. Regional web ACLs run at the ALB, Shield Advanced targets DDoS, and Network Firewall is a regional network-layer control. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/aws-managed-rule-groups-ip-rep.html

prompt: A company wants to rehost hundreds of VMware VMs onto Amazon EC2 quickly, keeping each machine's configuration as it is for now and optimizing later, with a short cutover window per wave. Which service fits best?

options.text: AWS Transform MGN (formerly Application Migration Service), replicating each VM's disks continuously until cutover to EC2.
VM Import/Export, exporting each VM as an OVA to S3 and importing it as an AMI during each wave's cutover.
options.explanation: Import is a one-time copy taken while the VM is stopped or changing, so each cutover waits for a full export and import.

options.text: AWS Server Migration Service, scheduling incremental replication of each VM's volumes into AMIs.
options.explanation: Server Migration Service was discontinued in 2022; AWS directs rehost migrations to MGN instead.

options.text: AWS DMS homogeneous migrations for the databases, and new app servers built from EC2 Image Builder recipes.
options.explanation: Rebuilding servers from recipes is a replatform, not a rehost, and it does not keep each machine's configuration.

explanation: MGN (now AWS Transform MGN, formerly AWS Application Migration Service) is the AWS rehost service: it replicates each source server's disks block by block continuously, so test and cutover instances launch on EC2 from an up-to-date copy and the cutover window is short. VM Import/Export is a one-off image copy, Server Migration Service is discontinued, and rebuilding servers changes their configuration. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/mgn/latest/ug/what-is-mgn.html

prompt: A Transit Gateway is associated with a Direct Connect gateway that has transit VIFs on two DX connections at different locations, and the TGW also has a Site-to-Site VPN attachment as backup. On premises advertises the same prefixes on all three paths. Traffic from AWS must use location 1, then location 2, then the VPN only if both DX paths are down. What achieves this?

options.text: Tag location 1's prefixes with community 7224:7300 and location 2's with 7224:7100, relying on the TGW preferring DX over VPN routes.
Tag location 1's prefixes with community 7224:7100 and location 2's with 7224:7300, relying on the TGW preferring DX over VPN routes.
options.explanation: 7224:7100 is the low preference community and 7224:7300 the high, so this makes location 2 the primary path.

options.text: Tag location 1's prefixes with 7224:7300 and location 2's with 7224:7100, and add static TGW routes for the prefixes to the VPN.
options.explanation: Static routes beat propagated routes in a TGW route table, so the VPN would carry the traffic even with both DX paths up.

options.text: Advertise more specific prefixes over the VPN and the summary prefixes over both VIFs, with AS_PATH prepended on location 2.
options.explanation: Longest prefix match is evaluated first, so the more specific VPN routes would win over both DX paths.

explanation: For traffic leaving AWS over Direct Connect, the local preference communities set on your advertisements decide between connections: 7224:7300 is high and 7224:7100 low, so location 1 becomes primary. In the Transit Gateway route table, with equal prefixes, routes propagated from a Direct Connect gateway are preferred over VPN routes, so the VPN is used only when no DX route remains. Static routes and longer prefixes override that preference. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/routing-and-bgp.html

prompt: Account admins in workload accounts may create IAM roles for their applications, but every role they create must carry the platform team's approved permissions boundary, and they must be unable to remove or weaken it later. Which TWO SCP statements belong in the design? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Deny iam:CreateRole and iam:PutRolePermissionsBoundary unless iam:PermissionsBoundary equals the approved boundary policy ARN.
Deny iam:DeleteRolePermissionsBoundary, and any edit of the approved boundary policy, to principals outside the platform team.
Deny iam:CreateRole to principals outside the platform team, which then creates each application role on request from admins.
options.explanation: This stops account admins from creating roles at all, which the requirement says they must be able to do.

options.text: Deny iam:PassRole unless the role being passed has a Boundary=Approved tag set when the role was created.
options.explanation: Admins can set any tag they like, and the tag says nothing about which boundary is attached, so nothing is enforced.

options.text: An IAM policy on each account's admin role that denies creating roles without the approved boundary.
options.explanation: This is not an SCP, and an account admin can detach or edit an IAM policy on their own role.

explanation: Delegating role creation safely needs two guarantees, both enforced by SCPs so account admins cannot undo them: roles can only be created (or have their boundary set) with the approved boundary, checked with the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition key, and nobody outside the platform team can delete a role's boundary or edit the boundary policy (CreatePolicyVersion, SetDefaultPolicyVersion, DeletePolicy). Tags and account-level IAM policies can be changed by the admins they target. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_boundaries.html

prompt: A payments platform in two Regions keeps its ledger in Aurora PostgreSQL, idempotency keys in DynamoDB, and queues work in SQS FIFO. Leadership wants both Regions to accept payments at all times, no payment ever charged twice, and a 5-minute RTO. What is the most defensible design?

options.text: Accept requests in both Regions, but send ledger writes and idempotency checks to one writer Region, with tested Aurora Global Database failover.
Aurora Global Database with write forwarding from the secondary, and idempotency keys in DynamoDB global tables using eventual consistency.
options.explanation: Each Region checks its own eventually consistent replica, so the same payment can pass the idempotency check in both Regions.

options.text: A separate Aurora cluster writing its own ledger in each Region, reconciled every few minutes by DMS bidirectional replication.
options.explanation: Two independent writers can both accept the same payment, and reconciling minutes later is too late to stop the double charge.

options.text: DynamoDB global tables as the ledger with last-writer-wins, and SQS FIFO deduplication IDs blocking repeat charges across Regions.
options.explanation: FIFO deduplication is per queue and per Region for five minutes, and last-writer-wins can silently drop a ledger write.

explanation: Exactly-once charging needs one place that serializes the idempotency check and the ledger write. Both Regions can take requests, but they forward those writes to a single writer Region; Aurora Global Database keeps a secondary ready to promote within minutes. Eventually consistent replicas, independent writers and SQS FIFO deduplication are all Region-local or asynchronous, so a retry hitting the other Region can be charged again. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/AuroraUserGuide/aurora-global-database.html

prompt: A central log bucket in a log archive account holds CloudTrail and VPC Flow Logs. Auditors require that the security operators who administer that account cannot delete logs before retention ends and cannot read them without approval from a separate security account. Which combination meets both requirements?

options.text: Object Lock in compliance mode, and SSE-KMS with a key held in the security account, whose key policy decides who may decrypt.
Object Lock in governance mode, and SSE-KMS with a key in the log archive account limited to a security role in its key policy.
options.explanation: Governance mode can be bypassed by anyone granted s3:BypassGovernanceRetention, and a same-account key can be re-permissioned.

options.text: Object Lock in compliance mode, SSE-S3 encryption, and MFA Delete on the bucket with CloudTrail management events.
options.explanation: Retention is protected, but SSE-S3 lets anyone with s3:GetObject read the logs; there is no separate approval for decryption.

options.text: Object Lock in compliance mode, and SSE-KMS with a key in the log archive account whose key policy lets the operators decrypt.
options.explanation: The operators already hold decrypt on a key in their own account, so they can read the logs without anyone's approval.

explanation: Compliance mode stops any user, the root user included, from deleting or shortening retention on a locked object version until it expires. Reading needs kms:Decrypt, so holding the key in the security account means the log archive operators can read only when the security account grants it, and each Decrypt call is logged by CloudTrail. Governance mode can be bypassed, and SSE-S3 or a same-account key leaves reading in the operators' hands. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html

prompt: A latency-sensitive Oracle RAC database runs an application that depends on several active database instances sharing storage. The business asks to 'move it to RDS tomorrow' with minimal code change. What should the architect recommend first?

options.text: Assess the app's RAC dependencies first, since no RDS option for Oracle supports RAC, and compare re-architecting with Oracle Database@AWS.
Migrate to RDS for Oracle Multi-AZ, whose synchronous standby gives the app the active instances it expects from RAC.
options.explanation: The Multi-AZ standby is passive and cannot serve traffic, so it does not provide RAC's multiple active instances.

options.text: Migrate to RDS Custom for Oracle, whose OS-level access lets the team install and configure Oracle RAC itself.
options.explanation: RDS Custom gives OS access to a single-instance database; it does not support Oracle RAC.

options.text: Load RDS for Oracle with AWS DMS, then point the app's RAC services at read replicas to spread the load.
options.explanation: RDS for Oracle read replicas are read-only, so they cannot take the writes the app sends to each RAC instance.

explanation: Neither RDS for Oracle nor RDS Custom for Oracle supports Real Application Clusters; Multi-AZ uses a passive standby and read replicas are read-only. An app that relies on several active instances on shared storage needs an assessment first: re-architect it to run on a single writer, or keep RAC on Oracle Database@AWS, which runs Oracle Exadata Database Service in AWS data centers. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Oracle.Concepts.FeatureSupport.html

prompt: A DynamoDB table in on-demand mode throttles writes. The partition key is tenantId and the sort key is a timestamp, and one tenant produces 70% of all writes. Which TWO changes address the throttling? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Write-shard the hot tenant by adding a calculated suffix to its partition key value, and query each suffix in parallel on read.
Redesign the partition key to combine tenantId with a high-cardinality attribute such as deviceId that the queries already use.
Switch the table to provisioned capacity with auto scaling and a maximum write capacity set well above current peaks.
options.explanation: Each partition is still capped at 1,000 write units per second, so raising table capacity does not help one hot key.

options.text: Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the table so writes for the hot tenant are absorbed by the cache.
options.explanation: DAX is a write-through cache: each write still goes to the table, so the hot partition sees the same load.

options.text: Add a global secondary index keyed on tenantId and timestamp so the hot tenant's writes are spread to the index.
options.explanation: The index has the same hot key, and a throttled GSI can throttle writes to the base table as well.

explanation: Every partition is limited to 1,000 write units per second whatever the table's capacity mode, so a key that takes 70% of writes throttles. Spreading that tenant's writes across several partition key values, either by write sharding with a suffix or by a higher-cardinality key the queries can still use, removes the hot spot. Table capacity, DAX and a GSI with the same key leave all writes on one key. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-partition-key-sharding.html

prompt: A global analytics platform's bill is dominated by inter-AZ transfer between chatty services, NAT gateway processing for traffic to S3, and cross-Region replication of raw data that is only queried after aggregation. Leadership asks for one quick discount. What is the best first response?

options.text: Break the bill down by usage type, then add an S3 gateway endpoint, keep chatty tiers AZ-local, and replicate aggregates, not raw data.
Buy a Compute Savings Plan sized to the current monthly bill, so the data transfer and NAT charges are billed at the plan rate.
options.explanation: Savings Plans discount compute usage; data transfer, NAT processing and S3 charges are not covered by them.

options.text: Move the chatty services into a single AZ per Region and add S3 interface endpoints to take the traffic off the NAT gateways.
options.explanation: This trades away AZ resilience, and interface endpoints add hourly and per-GB charges a free gateway endpoint avoids.

options.text: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the replicated raw data and buy Compute Savings Plans for the EC2 fleet before anything else.
options.explanation: Neither touches the transfer, NAT and replication charges that dominate the bill.

explanation: The dominant charges are data movement, which commitments do not discount. Breaking the bill down by usage type confirms the drivers; then an S3 gateway endpoint removes NAT processing for S3, AZ-affine routing between chatty tiers cuts inter-AZ transfer where resilience allows, and replicating aggregated data shrinks cross-Region transfer. Savings Plans can follow for the stable compute. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/cost-optimization-pillar/plan-for-data-transfer.html

prompt: A private hosted zone for corp.internal is associated with many VPCs, and on premises also hosts legacy records under corp.internal. After a Resolver forwarding rule for corp.internal was associated with the VPCs, the AWS-hosted records under corp.internal stopped resolving from them. What fixes this while keeping both sets of records resolvable?

options.text: Move the AWS records into a subdomain such as aws.corp.internal in its own zone, and keep forwarding corp.internal on premises.
Add a second outbound endpoint and more IP addresses to the existing one, so the forwarding rule has more capacity.
options.explanation: The queries are being answered by the forwarding rule as configured; capacity is not the problem.

options.text: Create a system rule for corp.internal so Resolver answers it from the private hosted zone, ending forwarding to on premises.
options.explanation: The AWS records resolve again, but the on-premises legacy records under corp.internal stop resolving from the VPCs.

options.text: Reassociate the private hosted zone with the VPCs after the rule, so the zone's newer association takes precedence.
options.explanation: Resolver does not rank by association order; for the same domain name a forwarding rule wins over a private hosted zone.

explanation: When a forwarding rule and a private hosted zone cover the same domain name, Resolver uses the forwarding rule, so the AWS-hosted names are sent on premises and fail. Resolver picks the most specific match, so giving the AWS records their own subdomain zone (aws.corp.internal) lets them resolve locally while everything else under corp.internal still forwards on premises. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/hosted-zone-private-considerations.html

prompt: A security account must administer AWS Security Hub, Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Config aggregation and IAM Access Analyzer for the whole organization. New accounts must be covered automatically, and the management account must stay out of day-to-day security operations. What is the cleanest pattern?

options.text: Register the security account as delegated administrator for each service, using each service's organization auto-enable where it exists.
Run each service from the management account with organization-wide auto-enable, limited to security staff by IAM policies.
options.explanation: This puts daily security operations in the management account, which is what the requirement rules out.

options.text: Make the security account delegated administrator for Security Hub alone, relying on its integrations to enable the other services.
options.explanation: Security Hub ingests findings from integrated services; it does not enable or administer GuardDuty, Config or Access Analyzer.

options.text: Use Control Tower Account Factory to deploy each service into new accounts, sending findings to the audit account by EventBridge.
options.explanation: Per-account deployments with event forwarding leave no central administrator for each service, so management stays distributed.

explanation: Each of these services integrates with AWS Organizations and supports a delegated administrator, which moves administration out of the management account; where the service offers organization auto-enable, new accounts are covered without extra work. Running from the management account breaks the requirement, Security Hub does not administer the other services, and per-account deployments have no central admin. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_integrate_services_list.html

prompt: A warm-standby DR test failed: DNS moved to the DR Region, but users saw stale data, and some writes accepted just before the switch were lost. Which TWO practices most directly prevent this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: When the primary is reachable, stop or drain writes there and wait for replication to catch up before promoting the DR database.
Monitor replication lag continuously, and have the runbook check it against the RPO before deciding to promote the DR copy.
Lower the TTL on the application's Route 53 records to 10 seconds so clients move to the DR Region sooner.
options.explanation: A shorter TTL moves clients faster, but they still reach a replica that has not caught up.

options.text: Scale the DR Region's application tier to full production size before the switch so it can take the full load at once.
options.explanation: Capacity helps the DR Region serve traffic; it does nothing about data that has not replicated yet.

options.text: Use Route 53 ARC routing controls so traffic shifts through an explicit, audited switch rather than health checks.
options.explanation: Routing controls make the traffic switch deliberate, but they do not sequence it with database replication.

explanation: Stale reads and lost writes come from promoting an asynchronous replica before it has caught up. A planned failover should stop writes at the primary and let replication drain before promotion, and the runbook needs current lag measured against the RPO to decide when promotion is acceptable. TTLs, capacity and routing controls change how traffic moves, not what data is in the DR Region. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html
